extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of mechanics, history and philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and epistemological standards for formulating and judging mechanical theories and principles (e.g., inertia, action principles, reference frames), as discussed in a mechanics textbook appendix.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience informs what is to be determined (empirical grounding)
rubrics_metrics.description: It first devolves on experience to inform us what particular dependence of phenomena on one another actually exists, what the thing to be determined is — and experience alone can instruct us on this point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use experience to identify which relations and quantities are relevant before formulating general laws; do not invent the object of determination purely a priori. Once adequate data are at hand and the phenomenon is judged sufficiently instructed by experience, one may regard it as uniquely determined and proceed without waiting for further experiments. Example: if experience shows bodies determine accelerations, then in absence of such bodies expect uniform motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical element plus a priori validity (inertia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heymans, Poske, and Petzoldt concur in finding an empirical and a supra-empirical element in the law of inertia; experience simply afforded the opportunity for applying an a priori valid principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that some principles may have both empirical origins and a priori applicability. The empirical component supplies the content; the a priori component supplies the general applicability once the content is fixed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of unique determination
rubrics_metrics.description: When adequate data are at hand we regard it as unnecessary to keep on waiting for further experiences; the phenomenon is determined for us, and since this alone is determination, it is uniquely determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat physical laws as statements of unique determination: given the relevant conditions, the outcome is uniquely fixed. This principle underlies deductions of equilibrium and dynamics and justifies equating variations to zero in variational formulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of least action / minimum principles as analytic expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of least action, like all other minimum principles in mechanics, is a simple expression of the fact that in the instances in question precisely so much happens as possibly can happen under the circumstances, or as is determined, viz., uniquely determined, by them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use variational/minimum principles as compact analytic formulations of unique determination. Recognize that Euler, Hamilton, and Gauss provide analytic expressions of this empirical fact. Ensure uniqueness of the minimum, since the uniqueness is what makes the principle determinative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use limiting cases / principle of continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceiving a body rolling down an inclined plane ... the retardation zero, or unending uniform motion on a horizontal plane, must have occurred to him. Galileo frequently employed consideration of limiting cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ limiting-case reasoning (continuity) to infer idealized laws (e.g., inertia) from sequences of concrete cases. Limiting cases are a legitimate heuristic and pedagogical device; failure to consider them can obscure fundamental insights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference frames must be physically demonstrable
rubrics_metrics.description: Direction and velocity which is taken into account in the law of inertia had no comprehensible meaning if the law was referred to absolute space. We can metrically determine direction and velocity only in a space of which the points are marked directly or indirectly by given bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formulate laws with respect to coordinate systems or reference frames that are anchored to observable bodies (earth, fixed stars) rather than to metaphysical absolute space. For motions of large spatio-temporal extent, reference to the fixed stars may be appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid metaphysical/unobservable assumptions (reject absolute motion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The elimination of absolute motion is equivalent to the elimination of what is physically meaningless ... A thing that is beyond the ken of knowledge, a thing that cannot be exhibited to the senses, has no meaning in natural science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not base physical theory on constructs that cannot be exhibited or measured. If a concept (e.g., absolute motion or an undistinguishable ether particle) has no experimental or metrical content, prefer formulations that avoid it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cautious use of thought-experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: When experimenting in thought, it is permissible to modify unimportant circumstances ... but it is not to be antecedently assumed that the universe is without influence on the phenomenon in question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use mental experiments to probe consequences, but do not make physically illegitimate assumptions (for example, removing all other bodies without considering their influence). Thought-experiments should respect plausible physical conditions and limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dynamical definition of mass
rubrics_metrics.description: After it has been discovered that the behavior of bodies toward one another is one in which accelerations are determined ... it is possible to give only one rational definition of mass, and that a purely dynamical definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define mass in terms of dynamical behavior (relations of accelerations and forces) rather than as an arbitrary or metaphysical attribute. From this definition, concepts like force and action–reaction follow naturally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metric determinability requirement for physical quantities
rubrics_metrics.description: As a matter of fact, we can metrically determine direction and velocity only in a space of which the points are marked directly or indirectly by given bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require that directional and speed measurements be tied to physically identifiable markers; avoid attributing metric meaning to quantities that lack such anchoring (this bears on debates about absolute space and orientation by ether).

rubrics_metrics.name: Work determines velocity; equilibrium via variation = 0
rubrics_metrics.description: If we have once perceived that the work A determines velocity, it will readily be seen that where work is not done when the system passes into all adjacent positions, no velocity can be acquired, and consequently that equilibrium obtains. The condition of equilibrium will therefore be δA = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use work/energy as the generator of motion: stationary values (no first variation) of the appropriate work/action functional correspond to equilibrium states. Apply variational calculus to determine equilibrium and dynamic equations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of thought as a methodological virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: My conception of economy of thought was developed out of my experience as a teacher ... It is merely incumbent on the individual to outline as distinctly as possible the main features of his own view of the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor explanations and formulations that are economical and clear, particularly in pedagogy and exposition. Strive to express main features distinctly and avoid unnecessary complications that do not contribute to understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer methods that make thought steps explicit (synthetic/geometric clarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Grassmann finds the main advantage of his procedure in the fact that every step in the calculation is at the same time the clear expression of every step taken in the thought; whereas, in the common method, the latter is forced entirely into the background by the introduction of three arbitrary co-ordinates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select analytic or synthetic methods that keep the intellectual steps visible (e.g., representing forces by line-segments, Hamilton/Grassmann methods). This improves clarity and pedagogical power compared with introducing arbitrary coordinates that hide the thought process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use abstraction and idealization but test their legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of inertia was enunciated as a dogma which accorded perfectly with the system ... It always remained remote and within the comprehension of supernatural genius only. Abstraction can reveal principles but one must ask whether assumptions (like removal of all obstacles) legitimately lead to the asserted consequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply abstraction and idealization (e.g., ignoring friction) to reveal underlying principles, but critically examine whether the idealized assumptions legitimately support the inferred laws. Beware of treating idealized results as dogma without justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic expressions (Euler/Hamilton/Gauss) are empirical in meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The theorems of Euler and Hamilton, and not less that of Gauss, are thus nothing more than analytic expressions for the fact of experience that the phenomena of nature are uniquely determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret formal analytic results as compact encodings of empirical facts of unique determination; ensure mathematical formalism remains tied to empirical content rather than being treated as purely abstract.
